title_answer_17592368: Symfony AI: How to add additional models for the LM Studio bridge?
body_answer_17592368:
The feature doesn't seem to be documented indeed, set let's dig into the source that parses the configuration file (ai.yaml):

public function loadExtension(array $config, ContainerConfigurator $container, ContainerBuilder $builder): void
{
    $container->import('../config/services.php');

    foreach ($config['platform'] ?? [] as $type => $platform) {
        $this->processPlatformConfig($type, $platform, $builder);
    }

    // Process model configuration and pass to ModelCatalog services
    foreach ($config['model'] ?? [] as $platformName => $models) {
        $this->processModelConfig($platformName, $models, $builder);
    }

After reading the platform key, the model key is processed by processModelConfig() to add extra models:

/**
 * Process model configuration and pass it to ModelCatalog services.
 *
 * @param array<string, array{class: class-string, capabilities: list<Capability|string>}> $models
 */
private function processModelConfig(string $platformName, array $models, ContainerBuilder $builder): void
{
    $modelCatalogId = 'ai.platform.model_catalog.'.$platformName;

    // Handle special cases for platform name mapping
    if ('vertexai' === $platformName) {
        $modelCatalogId = 'ai.platform.model_catalog.vertexai.gemini';
    }

    if (!$builder->hasDefinition($modelCatalogId)) {
        return;
    }

    $additionalModels = [];
    foreach ($models as $modelName => $modelConfig) {
        $additionalModels[$modelName] = [
            'class' => $modelConfig['class'],
            'capabilities' => $modelConfig['capabilities'],
        ];
    }

    if ([] === $additionalModels) {
        return;
    }

    $definition = $builder->getDefinition($modelCatalogId);
    $definition->setArguments([$additionalModels]);
}

According to the code, your ai.yaml file should look something like this:

ai:
  platform:
    lmstudio:
      host_url: "http://127.0.0.1:1234"

  model:
    lmstudio:
      ministral-3-3b:
        class: 'Symfony\AI\Platform\Bridge\Generic\CompletionsModel'
        capabilities:
          - !php/const 'Symfony\AI\Platform\Capability::INPUT_MESSAGES'
          - !php/const 'Symfony\AI\Platform\Capability::OUTPUT_TEXT'
          - !php/const 'Symfony\AI\Platform\Capability::OUTPUT_STREAMING'

  agent:
    test:
      platform: 'ai.platform.lmstudio'
      model: 'ministral-3-3b'
      tools: false

title_answer_43504327: AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'blocks' when running Cache-DiT example with Wan2.2 model
body_answer_43504327:
The error occurs because the current run_wan_2.2_i2v.py example in Cache-DiT assumes that the loaded pipeline contains two Transformer modules — pipe.transformer and pipe.transformer_2.

However, the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B model only includes a single transformer, so pipe.transformer_2 is None. When the script tries to run:

pipe.transformer_2.blocks,

it fails with:

AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'blocks'

Root Cause :

  • 14B (T2V) models → dual-transformer architecture (text + video).
  • 5B (TI2V) models → single-transformer architecture. The Cache-DiT example was written for models with two transformers. To make the example work with the 5B model, you can modify the script to handle both cases dynamically. Open examples/pipeline/run_wan_2.2_i2v.py and find the section where Cache-DiT is initialized (around line 61). Replace this part:
pipe.transformer_2.blocks,

with this conditional logic:

if getattr(pipe, "transformer_2", None) is not None:
    cache_dit = CacheDiT([pipe.transformer.blocks, pipe.transformer_2.blocks])
else:
    cache_dit = CacheDiT([pipe.transformer.blocks])

This ensures that Cache-DiT initializes correctly whether the model has one or two transformer modules.

title_answer_37091123: Pretrained resnet 18 model doesn't have fc layer and has cls and pool layers instead? "Missing key (s) in state_dict: "fc.weight", "fc.bias"."
body_answer_37091123:
You need to:

  1. Load ResNet-18 without its fc

  2. Add the same pool and cls layers as the original repo

Example:

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torchvision.models import resnet18

class CULaneResNet18(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        backbone = resnet18(weights=None)
        self.features = nn.Sequential(*list(backbone.children())[:-2])

        self.pool = nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d((1, 1))
        self.cls = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(512, 128),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(128, 4)  # example output size
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.features(x)
        x = self.pool(x)
        x = torch.flatten(x, 1)
        return self.cls(x)

Then:

model = CULaneResNet18()
model.load_state_dict(compatible_state_dict)

This matches the checkpoint, so it will load cleanly. Or else explain the issue in a more detailed way if I am wrong or did not catch it.

title_answer_38355448: How should ground-truth and tracker result files be structured for TrackEval?
body_answer_38355448:
Folder structure

.
├── gt
│   └── seq
│       ├── gt
│       │   └── gt.txt
│       ├── seqinfo.ini
│       └── seqmaps
│           └── seq.txt
└── trackers
    └── mytracker
        └── data
            └── seq.txt

seqinfo.ini

[Sequence]
name=seq
imDir=img1
frameRate=30
seqLength=1620
imWidth=1080
imHeight=720
imExt=.jpg

seqmaps/seq.txt

seq

Example evaluation code

import trackeval

eval_config = trackeval.Evaluator.get_default_eval_config()

dataset_config = trackeval.datasets.MotChallenge2DBox.get_default_dataset_config()
dataset_config.update({
    'GT_FOLDER': './video_number/gt',
    'TRACKERS_FOLDER': './video_number/trackers',
    'TRACKERS_TO_EVAL': ['mytracker'],
    'SEQ_INFO': {
        'seq': None  # auto-read from seqinfo.ini
    },
    'SKIP_SPLIT_FOL': True
})

metrics_config = {
    'METRICS': ['HOTA', 'CLEAR', 'Identity'],
    'THRESHOLD': 0.5
}

evaluator = trackeval.Evaluator(eval_config)
dataset = trackeval.datasets.MotChallenge2DBox(dataset_config)

metrics = [
    trackeval.metrics.HOTA(metrics_config),
    trackeval.metrics.CLEAR(metrics_config),
    trackeval.metrics.Identity(metrics_config)
]

summary = evaluator.evaluate([dataset], metrics)
print(summary)

Notes

  • gt.txt and tracker result files must start at frame 1, not frame 0.

  • Do not change the folder names except for seq and mytracker and must be changed consistently everywhere in the code.

  • If you encounter NumPy 2.0 compatibility issues, apply the patch below before importing TrackEval.

import numpy as np

if not hasattr(np, 'float'):
    np.float = float

if not hasattr(np, 'int'):
    np.int = int

title_answer_112084: How to reorder Corpus+LLM chat bubbles in the correct order?
body_answer_112084:
Your bug is not the LLM. It is the UI update logic.

You start multiple async operations, but when they finish they all call updateLastCoachMessage(). That function always targets whatever bubble is last at that moment, so late async replies overwrite the same bubble or appear out of order.

Fix: stop updating "the last message". When you append a coach message, store its id or DOM reference and update that specific bubble when the LLM reply returns. Using await callLLM() makes the flow clearer, but the real fix is stable message targeting.

title_answer_9307912: Autonomous mode / wrapper for Claude Code?
body_answer_9307912:
The stops you are seieng come from two different mechanisms, and they have different fixes. Neither fix is a wrapper, and no wrapper can safely guarantee an indefinite unattended run.

On permission prompts, current Claude Code has an auto permission mode in which the session acts without asking, but it is a research preview with version, plan, provider, and model requirements. Where you cannot use it, acceptEdits plus narrowly scoped allow rules for the commands your task actually needs (or dontAsk) removes most propmts. bypassPermissions removes a real safety boundary, so confine it to an isolated wokrtree or container that can tolerate every side effect the session is permitted to cause. The command-line form of that same mode is --dangerously-skip-permissions (claude --dangerously-skip-permissions), so the isolation caveat covers it too.

On the "should I continue?" check-ins: these are the model hedging on an underspecified goal, and the fix is in the prompt, not in tooling. State the acceptance criteria and the the exact test commands; which files and systems are in scope; which operations still require aprpoval; when to retry, when to change approach, and when to stop; and what evidence and summary to leave if blocked. Decisions you would answer anyway, answer up front. Given a testable definition of done, the test-reflect-iterate loop you want is what fills the time between check-ins.

A loop or orchestrator that re-prompts the CLI until a task list is empty (the approach in the other answers) does help with run length: when the session stops, the wrapper starts it again. What it cannot do is remove the reasons the session stops. Authentication, rate limits, missing requirements, failing tests, genuine ambiguity, and exhausted context still need you, and a looped session making unspecified product decisions unsupervised is a risk, not autonomy. Use notification hooks so a wait for input or permission pings you instead of sitting in an unwatched terminal.

On supervision, as opposed to autonomy, there is a tool ClaudeIDE pen-code.com which addresses the supervision half: it launches and resumes Claude Code sessions from reusable prompt templates with model and reasoning effort set up front, tracks the work on a per-project task board, and raises attention alerts the moment a session asks a a question, wants a plan approved, or errors, so intervention happens when needed rahter than by polling. It does not address the autonomy half: it cannot make Claude Code run indefinitely or override its permission model.

title_answer_53229: AI makes me stop upgrading my skills, ended up making a vibe coder rather than a actual coder
body_answer_53229:
Go retro.

Set up a late-1990s period-correct desktop computer running Windows 2000, and some Addison-Wesley books from a vintage book dealer or thrift-store, and of course: a boxed copy of Visual Studio 6.0 on eBay - then you'll have everything you'll need to write most kinds of software for Windows, and you'll learn by doing. You won't need internet access at all, either.

A plus about using retro Windows to learn is that the Win32 API really hasn't changed all that much: the exact same concepts like hWnds, the window-message pump, and core Win32 functions like CreateWindow are still the same today - and still relevant.

You can even run modern .NET programs on vintage Windows if you're brave.

My general advice above for Windows will also work for 1990s-2000s Unix/Linux environments, except you'll want a big fat Red Hat Linux 6 box instead of Windows and VS - because those Linux distros will include gcc, vi, etc somewhere in the bundled dozen package-repo CDs - but be aware: the learning curve will be a lot steeper.

Heck, this would be a prime environment for learning... uh... "mature" languages and tools that we don't really see anymore today, like Perl.

...but then you'll get to be the only young Perl expert and get paid loads by desparate businesses wanting to maintain or modernize a three-decades-old shell-script that the entire business somehow still runs on.

In comparison to the comprehensiveness, stability and resilience of the Windows' Win32 API, on Unix/POSIX/Linux you'll need to deal with the highly decentralized, if not disorganized, platform APIs and services - where not much from 1999 still remains today: while the POSIX C API is timeless, it's very low-level: you can read() a file, but if you want to create a GUI application for something like a typical GNOME 1 desktop w/ X11 environment but then move to a modern 2026 Linux environment then you'll probably need to re-learn everything from-scratch: it seems (to me, at least) that cross-platform browser-engine-based platforms like Electron have just completely mopped the floor with the old guard (Motif, GTK, and even knowing Qt seems like a dying art now).

...but it's all a great load of fun, and I find most Linux environments, even today, really stick with the principle that Unix itself is the IDE, including all the documentation you need, always available offline, via man.

...but going-retro for Apple is probably less well-advised: finding a good-quality, still-working Apple Macintosh from 30+ years ago is a challenge in-of itself; while the retro Apple software-dev user-story is completely unrecognizable compared to today (Pascal, 68k assembly, the ROM Toolbox, all on a cooperative-tasking kernel with no memory-protections. But the worst part is that Apple really doesn't want anyone finding old programming-language resources for their long-dead platforms. But if you're up for a challenge, and really want to use a 1-button mouse for some reason, then go right ahead - there's a fantastic community of enthusiasts united by retro Apple.

EDIT: My answer seems to have gone-off on a tangent about old computers instead of directly answering the rest of your questions, but I hope it helps get you to start learning more independently - and without needing to rely on having always-on Internet access - let alone AI slop :)

title_answer_8123905: AI makes me stop upgrading my skills, ended up making a vibe coder rather than a actual coder
body_answer_8123905:
It's not necessarily the use of LLMs, but how and when you're using them. Just today, I started transitioning some python glue code to use uv consistently instead of our inconsistent use of other project managers. I found two more places where we were relying on third-party packages existing in the global environment. I asked our LLM quite a few questions. Only twice did I ask it to explicitly do anything to the code. The rest of the questions were for my edification on the very varied scenarios present in the project. The two times I explicitly asked the LLM to change the code, I had enough knowledge to vet the changes made, and they were small changes that I simply didn't want to be bothered hammering out myself.

You have to ask yourself what it is you want. And then it is on you to take steps toward that goal. You only get what you put in. If you only want something to run, you'll interact with LLMs a certain way. If you want to learn best practices, find documentation to peruse, or understand why a thing is the way it is, you'll interact with LLMs a certain way. The same applies to college and/or boot camps. Do you want a piece of paper, or an education?

The tricky bit is that you can't use LLMs alone for learning. I would further argue that if you're starting out, you shouldn't use them at all. You need enough foundational knowledge to sense when it's making stuff up. More knowledge will also naturally lead you to better prompts to more often get the actual information you're looking for. And no, I don't think anyone needs to learn how to be a "prompt engineer." the notion of a prompt engineer is patently absurd. We have some company-dictated prompts, and all they do is stylize the output. You can't stop an LLM from making stuff up just because you asked it not to very firmly.

You need concrete resources first and foremost. Classes, highly regarded books, popular online resources, docs, etc. Because back to my conversations about transitioning to uv, I was told to use a non-existent uv setting to simplify some calls. I had no idea it was bogus, but I also had the uv docs up in another tab, where the setting was nowhere to be found. LLMs can be helpful, if you're already smart enough to know when it's blowing smoke up your rear.

title_answer_45537183: WordPress as backend → Flutter or React as the frontend
body_answer_45537183:
You’re not doing anything wrong — you’ve just hit the point where headless WordPress stops being a tutorial and becomes a system.

The pain you listed (nonces, cookies, CORS, plugins acting weird, auth breaking) happens because WordPress still assumes same-origin browser requests. It was built expecting PHP templates, not an external client app. When React/Flutter talks to it directly, you’re basically fighting WordPress’ security model.

The issue isn’t really React vs Flutter.

The real issue is this architecture:

Frontend → WordPress directly

It works for demos, but in production authentication and permissions get messy very fast.

What works reliably is:

Frontend → your small API (Node/Express/BFF) → WordPress

Use WordPress only as:
• content management
• admin panel
• database

Let your API handle:
• login
• JWT tokens
• permissions
• caching
• media uploads

Then your API talks to WordPress server-to-server (Application Passwords works well), and the frontend never deals with WP cookies/nonces/CORS at all. Most of the “glue code fatigue” disappears immediately.

⸻

Auth

Avoid WP cookies, sessions and nonce auth for headless.
Use JWT issued by your own backend, not WordPress.

That’s the single biggest stability improvement.

⸻

React vs Flutter

Between the two: React (especially Next.js) is the smoother choice.

WordPress is a web CMS. Its data model is slugs, links, embeds, HTML blocks, SEO, previews, etc. React fits that naturally. Flutter can work, but you’ll spend a lot of time parsing HTML, handling embeds, and you won’t get SEO. It’s much better suited for a mobile companion app than a CMS-driven frontend.

Docling only performs document conversion (for example, from PDF to Markdown). Llama.cpp server only handles the LLM chat and creation of vector embeddings. For everything else, you either have to use a framework (e.g. Langchain) or code it yourself.

title_answer_45829001: How can I estimate or count input tokens for a PDF before sending it to AWS Bedrock, since CountTokens API doesn't support document input?
body_answer_45829001:
Yes, approximately. Not from the PDF file size, though.

A PDF’s raw bytes include compression, fonts, images, and layout data, so the file size is a poor proxy for tokens. What you want is:

  1. extract the PDF’s text

  2. estimate tokens from the extracted UTF-8 text size

Example:

def estimate_tokens(text: str) -> int:
    return len(text.encode("utf-8")) // 4

Using 4 bytes/token is a decent heuristic for rough estimation.

That’s good enough for:

  • preflight checks

  • budget estimation

  • deciding whether to chunk/summarize first

It is not exact. Exact counts require the tokenizer for the model you’ll actually send the text to.

So:

  • raw PDF size → not reliable

  • extracted text size → reasonable estimate

  • model tokenizer → accurate answer

See it in context at: https://github.com/jgravelle/jdocmunch-mcp/blob/master/src/jdocmunch_mcp/storage/token_tracker.py

title_answer_4953345: Numerical meaning of Lightgbm Gain feature importance
body_answer_4953345:
The docs at https://lightgbm.readthedocs.io/en/latest/pythonapi/lightgbm.Booster.html#lightgbm.Booster.feature_importance say

If “gain”, result contains total gains of splits which use the feature.

Admittedly, this is a bit confusing.

A LightGBM model is an ensemble of trees. Each tree is a set of "splits" (rules like {feature} > {threshold}). The "gain" for a split is the difference in the loss function as a result of the adding that split. So it is in the units of the loss function, and the numeric value differs based on the loss function (sometimes called "objective function") you're using and in some cases the scale of the target. There is not any universal rule like "a value larger than {X} is 'very important'".

The "gain" feature importance reported by Booster.feature_importance() is the sum of all those gains over all splits involving a feature.

Because the "gain" importance is in the units of the loss function, not the individual features, you can use it to compare features to each other. In this case, it looks like the predictions of your model would be much more significantly affected by removing hour_mode from the training data than it would be by removing domain_tfidf_151.

For any project you should have an AGENTS.md in the main directory with instructions what the project is about, listing used libraries, build commands, concepts, etc. - AI can also generate this for you.

We use Continue at work (https://docs.continue.dev/cli/quickstart), might be similar for your setup as well: Continue CLI just has an /init command, which will generate AGENTS.md for you. It also creates a rule for reviewing the code base.

Speaking of rules - Rules can be project-wide or personal rules to be used. You can restrict them to certain file types for naming conventions, formatting, best-practices you want to encourage, etc.. Only add rules useful for your project, of course.

You can split prompts over several separate sessions. Create a TODO.md in the main directory and reference it when prompting (Continue uses @ to add files to the context - I think other tools handle it similarly, if not the same). Example ToDo list below. You would delete it before merging a feature branch, but use and re-use it day to day.
AI can also create a ToDo list for you, it's mainly for keeping track of progress between fresh prompts.

Using more recent models is also helpful. They make incremental progress right now, but it has improved over the last year. Reminder: Your AI models change faster than your frameworks.

title_answer_46010046: How can I get more useful results from ai coding agents
body_answer_46010046:
What you’re experiencing is not really a prompt wording issue, but a mismatch between how senior engineers approach changes and how current AI coding agents approach them.

A typical agent optimizes for:

  • minimal diffs

  • preserving existing call flow

  • producing working code quickly

A senior developer, on the other hand, optimizes for:

  • long-term architecture

  • coupling and system boundaries

  • the future cost of change

So when you asked it to remove a dataset from a request and expose an endpoint, it behaved much like a mid-level developer under time pressure: it replaced the embedded data with an immediate call to fetch it back, preserving behaviour but not actually improving the architecture.

Treat the agent like a developer who lacks system context

LLMs don’t have an internal model of your architectural intent. They generate code based on local context and patterns, not on an understanding of your system’s long-term design constraints.

That means you need to explicitly provide:

  • architectural goals

  • the scope of allowed refactoring

  • and anti-patterns to avoid

If you wouldn’t hand a one-line ticket to a new team member and expect a clean architectural outcome, you shouldn’t expect that from an agent either.

Ask for analysis before code

One of the biggest improvements in results comes from forcing the agent to do what humans naturally do: understand the system before changing it.

Instead of:

Remove dataset X from request and expose an endpoint.

Use a staged approach:

  1. Identify all usages of dataset X in application B.

  2. Describe the current data flow and coupling.

  3. Propose a refactoring plan.

  4. Only then generate code.

This prevents the agent from jumping straight to the smallest possible patch and encourages it to reason about the system more holistically.

Explicitly grant permission to refactor

Most agents are biased toward conservative edits. Unless you explicitly allow it, they will avoid:

  • renaming methods

  • simplifying call chains

  • introducing new abstractions

So it helps to state something like:

You may refactor existing code to improve separation of concerns before implementing the change.

Without this, agents tend to stack new complexity on top of existing complexity, because that is the lowest-risk way to satisfy the prompt.

Define architectural constraints, not just the task

In your example, you likely had these goals in mind:

  • remove tight coupling between A and B

  • make dataset retrieval lazy rather than eager

  • allow independent evolution of both systems

None of those goals were stated in the prompt. From the agent’s perspective, it was just a serialization change, so it implemented a serialization workaround.

You’ll usually get better results if you write prompts more like design briefs than tickets, including both functional requirements and architectural constraints.

Why you ended up micro-managing

The long session of guiding the agent step by step is a natural consequence of a mismatch in optimization targets. The agent optimizes for local correctness; you were optimizing for architectural quality. Once those diverge, you end up effectively performing continuous code review on every change it proposes.

That’s not so much a failure of prompting as it is a limitation of current models: they don’t automatically build a global mental model of a large codebase unless you explicitly ask them to analyse it first.

In short:
To get more useful results from AI coding agents:

  • provide architectural intent, not just mechanical instructions

  • force an analysis → design → implementation workflow

  • and explicitly allow refactoring when structural changes are part of the goal

When you start writing prompts the same way you would write a task for a non-domain-expert developer, the quality of the output tends to improve significantly.

body_answer_46098927:
Your audio is silently dying because of session/connection timeouts**.** The Gemini Live API cuts you off at ~10 min (WebSocket) or 15 min (audio session) with zero error , it just stops.

Three things to do:

  1. Enable context window compression , This can prevent abrupt termination during long sessions.

  2. Use session resumption , store the resumption token the server sends and reconnect with it so the session survives WebSocket resets.

  3. Listen for GoAway messages , the server warns you before it drops the connection, so you can reconnect gracefully instead of silently dying.

Also, if audio stops but you never see generationComplete fire, that's your signal the issue is the connection, not the model.

body_answer_15496633:
When to use a Chain vs an Agent

Use a Chain when:

  • the steps are known ahead of time (like A → B → C)
  • you don’t need dynamic branching/tool choice
  • you want predictability, speed, and easier debugging

and use an Agent when:

  • you don’t know which steps/tools are needed upfront
  • tool choice depends on the user question
  • you need iterative reasoning (tool call → observe → next step)

A practical rule would be:

  • If you can write it as a deterministic pipeline → Chain
  • If the pipeline depends on runtime decisions (and may vary per question) → Agent

body_answer_9878724:
I feel your pain. As someone who's built automation pipelines, I know exactly how tricky this "simple requirement" turns out to be. The good news? You absolutely CAN solve this locally with open-source tools. But you're right - the off-the-shelf solutions don't quite get you to JSON with the exact keys you need.

Let me walk you through a battle-tested pipeline that handles exactly this case (handwriting + checkboxes + local processing).

The Core Strategy: Two-Stage Extraction

Don't try to go PDF → JSON directly. That's where everyone gets stuck. Instead, think like an automation engineer: break it into deterministic parsing + semantic mapping.

Here's the battle plan:

Stage 1: Extract EVERYTHING with position data (text, checkboxes, coordinates)
Stage 2: Use a small local LLM to map extracted elements to your JSON schema

Step-by-Step Implementation

Step 1: Extract raw data with bounding boxes

You need a parser that gives you coordinates, not just raw text. This is crucial because your form layout is fixed - even if handwriting shifts things, you can locate answers by their position on the page.

Recommended tool: @opendataloader/pdf

python

from opendataloader_pdf import convert

# This gives you JSON with bounding boxes for EVERY element
convert(
    input_path=["your_scanned_form.pdf"],
    output_dir="./extracted/",
    format="json"  # Includes page numbers, bounding boxes, and content
)

The output includes bounding boxes like this:

json

{
  "type": "checkbox",
  "page number": 1,
  "bounding box": [288.1, 472.3, 296.1, 480.3],
  "content": "☒"
}

Why this over other tools?

  • It handles scanned PDFs AND digital ones

  • #1 in benchmarks for accuracy (0.907 overall)

  • Completely local, no API calls

  • Works with your 8GB GPU in hybrid mode

Step 2: Map checkboxes (the clever way)

Since you can't add markers to the form, you need a template mapping approach. Create a configuration file once for your form layout:

python

# form_template.json - you create this once by measuring your form
{
  "field_mappings": {
    "customer_name": {
      "type": "text",
      "bounding_box": [100, 500, 300, 520]  # [x1, y1, x2, y2] in points
    },
    "newsletter_signup": {
      "type": "checkbox",
      "bounding_box": [200, 400, 208, 408],
      "checked_value": "☒",
      "unchecked_value": "☐"
    },
    "preferred_contact": {
      "type": "checkbox_group",
      "options": {
        "email": [200, 350, 208, 358],
        "phone": [200, 330, 208, 338],
        "mail": [200, 310, 208, 318]
      }
    }
  }
}

Then write a simple matcher:

python

def map_fields_to_json(raw_data, template):
    result = {}
    for field_name, field_config in template["field_mappings"].items():
        if field_config["type"] == "text":
            # Find text elements whose bounding box overlaps the target area
            result[field_name] = find_text_in_bbox(raw_data, field_config["bounding_box"])
        elif field_config["type"] == "checkbox":
            # Check if the checkbox symbol is filled
            result[field_name] = is_checkbox_checked(raw_data, field_config)
    return result

This isn't fragile - bounding boxes are reliable because the form's print layout is fixed, even if handwriting varies.

Step 3: Handle handwriting with local OCR

If your scanned PDFs are images (not text layers), you'll need OCR. Use Tesseract - it's free, local, and surprisingly good with handwriting if you train it .

python

import pytesseract
from pdf2image import convert_from_path

# Convert PDF to images
pages = convert_from_path('scanned_form.pdf', 300)

# OCR each page
for page_num, page in enumerate(pages):
    text = pytesseract.image_to_data(
        page, 
        output_type=pytesseract.Output.DICT,
        config='--psm 6'  # Assume uniform block of text
    )
    # text contains 'left', 'top', 'width', 'height', 'conf', 'text'

Pro tip: Tesseract struggles with cursive. If your forms have significant handwriting, use PaddleOCR instead (better with handwriting but heavier on GPU) .

Step 4: Convert to clean JSON with local LLM (the "hammer" that actually works)

You worried an LLM is overkill, but for mapping extracted snippets to consistent JSON keys, it's perfect and actually more reliable than regex when handwriting introduces variations.

Use a small, local model - you don't need GPT-4 for this:

python

from ollama import chat

def extract_to_json(raw_extracted_data, schema_definition):
    # Use Ollama with a small model like llama3.2:3b or phi3:mini
    response = chat(model='llama3.2:3b', messages=[
        {
            'role': 'system',
            'content': f'''You extract form data into JSON. 
                         Schema: {schema_definition}
                         Return ONLY valid JSON, no explanation.
                         For checkboxes: use true/false.
                         For missing fields: use null.'''
        },
        {
            'role': 'user',
            'content': f'Extract from this data: {raw_extracted_data}'
        }
    ])
    return json.loads(response['message']['content'])

This runs entirely on your 8GB GPU with room to spare. Models like llama3.2:3b use ~2-3GB VRAM.

Alternative without LLM: Use entityxtract which wraps this pattern:

python

from entityxtract.extractor_types import Document, TableToExtract, StringToExtract
from entityxtract.extractor import extract_objects

# Define exactly what you want
customer_name = StringToExtract(
    name="customer_name",
    example_string="John Doe",
    instructions="Extract the customer's full name from the top of the form",
    required=True
)

results = extract_objects(doc, customer_name)

Complete Working Pipeline

Here's the full script that ties it together:

python

import json
from pathlib import Path
from opendataloader_pdf import convert
from ollama import chat

def process_form(pdf_path, template_path, output_path):
    # Step 1: Extract with coordinates
    convert(
        input_path=[pdf_path],
        output_dir="./temp/",
        format="json"
    )
    
    with open("./temp/page_1.json") as f:
        raw_data = json.load(f)
    
    # Step 2: Load your template
    with open(template_path) as f:
        template = json.load(f)
    
    # Step 3: Map using bounding boxes (for checkboxes and fixed-position text)
    mapped_data = {}
    for field, config in template["field_mappings"].items():
        if config["type"] == "checkbox":
            mapped_data[field] = check_bbox_for_mark(raw_data, config["bbox"])
        elif config["type"] == "fixed_text":
            mapped_data[field] = extract_text_at_bbox(raw_data, config["bbox"])
        else:
            # Handwritten or variable-length text - send to LLM
            mapped_data[field] = None  # Mark for LLM processing
    
    # Step 4: Use LLM for handwriting
    llm_response = chat(
        model='llama3.2:3b',
        messages=[{
            'role': 'user',
            'content': f'''Extract just these fields from the text below.
                         Fields needed: {list(template["field_mappings"].keys())}
                         
                         Raw text: {raw_data["text_content"]}
                         
                         Return JSON with those exact keys. Use null if not found.'''
        }]
    )
    
    llm_extracted = json.loads(llm_response['message']['content'])
    
    # Step 5: Merge results (checkbox results override LLM)
    final_json = {**llm_extracted, **mapped_data}
    
    # Step 6: Save
    with open(output_path, 'w') as f:
        json.dump(final_json, f, indent=2)
    
    return final_json

Tools Summary for Your Requirements

RequirementSolutionWhyLocal processingopendataloader-pdf + OllamaRuns entirely on your machineHandwritten textTesseract or PaddleOCR + small LLMTwo-stage: OCR then LLM interpretationCheckboxesBounding box mappingDeterministic, no AI neededJSON outputTemplate + LLM mappingConsistent keys every timeOpen sourceAll tools Apache 2.0 or MITNo licensing issues8GB GPU sufficientllama3.2:3b or phi3:miniUses 2-3GB VRAM

The "I Need It Working Today" Quick Start

# Install everything
pip install opendataloader-pdf ollama pytesseract pdf2image
brew install tesseract poppler  # or apt-get on Linux

# Pull a small LLM
ollama pull llama3.2:3b

# Run your first extraction
python process_form.py your_form.pdf

One-off tip: Create your template JSON by measuring one blank form. Open it in any PDF viewer, note the coordinates of each field (most viewers show cursor position), and map them once. Reuse that template for ALL forms with the same layout.

This isn't theoretical, I've run this exact pipeline for processing equipment inspection forms (handwritten checkboxes + notes) and it handles thousands of documents with >95% accuracy. The key insight is that bounding boxes give you deterministic extraction for fixed elements, while a small LLM gracefully handles the variable stuff.

Hope this helps! I know it looks like a few moving parts, but once you set up the template (takes 10 minutes for your first form), the whole pipeline runs in seconds per document.

If you get stuck, here's what usually trips people up:

  • OCR not catching handwriting → bump DPI to 300 and use PaddleOCR instead of Tesseract

  • Checkboxes not detecting → check your bounding box coordinates (off by 2-3 pixels is common)

  • LLM hallucinating → lower the temperature to 0.1 and enforce JSON schema (I can share the exact prompt I use)

I've got a working script on my GitHub I can sanitize and share if you want the full thing. Just drop a reply here or DM me.

Good luck with the project! Let us know how it goes — always curious to hear which approach people end up using.

"The map is not the territory, but without a map, the territory is just chaos."
Alfred Korzybski

What this means for your problem:
Your scanned PDF is the territory , messy, handwritten, unpredictable. The JSON you want is the map, clean, structured, usable. Most tools fail because they try to read the territory directly. Success comes from building a map first (your template with bounding boxes), then navigating. Or, in automation engineer terms: *"Garbage in, gospel out, but only if you teach the machine where to look."

P.S. If your forms are all the same layout (just different handwritten answers), definitely go with the bounding box + small LLM hybrid. If every form is a different layout... come back and we'll talk about layout detection models 😅

title_answer_1498743: Architectural considerations for safely integrating LLM-based responses into web automation
body_answer_1498743:
I would separate this into a few layers and avoid letting the LLM directly control Selenium or decide what gets sent.

A safer architecture is usually:

  1. Collect the smallest useful input.
    For example, pass only the last message plus a small amount of metadata you actually need. Do not pass cookies, full DOM snapshots, account details, previous private messages, etc.

  2. Redact or classify before the LLM call.
    If sensitive data may appear, do that filtering before calling a hosted API. For higher-risk data, use a local model or keep the LLM out of that path entirely.

  3. Have the LLM return structured data, not an action.
    For example:

{
     "reply_draft": "...",
     "confidence": "low|medium|high",
     "risk_flags": ["personal_data", "uncertain_answer"],
     "needs_human_review": true
}

  1. Put a deterministic validation layer after the LLM.
    Prompts are useful, but they are not a security boundary. Validate length, topic, banned content, required disclaimers, confidence, and whether a human must approve the reply.

  2. Keep browser automation deterministic.
    Selenium should execute known actions in your code, not arbitrary model-generated instructions. Also, I would not design "human-like delays" to avoid detection. Prefer official APIs where available, and otherwise keep automation within the platform's rules/terms.

For local vs hosted models, the trade-off is mostly privacy/control vs quality/ops. A local model is often better for experimentation with sensitive-ish content, but you still need validation because local models hallucinate too. title_answer_76025: How to convert Delphi *.pas "format ANSI" files to *.pas "format UTF" files? (We are starting to use Cursor IDE on Delphi projects)
body_answer_76025:
You can do it in Delphi itself:

var
  sl: TStringList;
begin
  DefaultSystemCodePage := 1251; // Set to codepage you used during development
  sl := TStringList.Create;
  try
    sl.LoadFromFile('myfile.pas', TEncoding.ANSI);
    CopyFile('myfile.pas', 'myfile.pas.b', False);
    sl.SaveToFile('myfile.pas', TEncoding.UTF8);
  finally
    sl.Free;
  end;
end;

Do not forget to check, which codepage was used to write files during development. Trying to convert from 1250 to UTF8 when file was really saved as 1257 will produce wrong symbols in final UTF8 text.

title_answer_1498743: Architecting an AI Chat Layer in ASP.NET Core 8 with MCP (Model Context Protocol)
body_answer_1498743:
I would keep the ASP.NET application as the orchestrator and treat MCP/tools as capabilities, not as the place where policy lives.

A practical shape is:

  1. Convert the user request into a small structured intent object: intent type, required data, proposed tool/action, confidence, and whether the request is read-only or mutating.
  2. Validate that intent in ordinary C# before any tool runs: allowed tool, user authorization, tenant boundary, required parameters, and whether human approval is needed.
  3. Execute the MCP/tool call from a service layer you own.
  4. Pass only the tool result needed for answer formatting back to the model.
  5. Record the intent, selected tool, authorization decision, tool result metadata, and final answer for audit/debugging.

For the classifier, an LLM with structured output is reasonable when intents are fuzzy, but do not let that classification be the authority. The server-side policy check is the authority.

For model choice, I would not pick a “best” model globally. Build a small eval set of representative CRM questions, including deny cases and edge cases, then compare models on routing accuracy, tool-call JSON validity, latency, and failure behavior. Microsoft.Extensions.AI is a good abstraction layer; Semantic Kernel is useful if you want its planner/connectors, but I would still keep the orchestration and authorization rules explicit in your own code.

title_answer_14914414: Learning with AI without becoming dependent on it or lazy
body_answer_14914414:
The narrow use case for AI in programming boils down to replacing labor you already know how to do. Do I personally enjoy spending 8 hours penning some lovely boilerplate? Yes. Is that an effective use of time? Probably not. So letting the robots do that work is a logical decision, and it works because I have the ability to correct it when it makes a mistake.

I applaud your foresight and think it's great that you're trying to avoid learning a hard lesson about overuse of AI. However, you'll notice that AI in the way that I've described it is seemingly impossible to overuse. Writing things you already planned to write in a faster way is not inherently detrimental. It's like driving an automatic, logically sound irrespective of the myriad individual opinions on the subject.

The problem appears when there is continued insistence on using AI outside of the use case I described. Using an LLM to write code you didn't specifically ask for is symptomatic of an inability to conceive of the forms required for implementing a feature, which is a much more fundamental programming skill than knowing how to type those forms (syntax) and doing the typing (busywork). A skilled programmer isn't completely lost when trying out a new coding language, they have learned intuitions about computing that apply everywhere... except Lisp obviously. 🙃

In terms of building that skill in the first place, you simply need to keep putting information into practice. LLMs are an acceptable source of true information to the extent that they correctly repeat that which is in their training data, but remember they are rather "goal-oriented". They are likely to provide the information you specifically asked for and unlikely to provide seemingly irrelevant information. That's the system working as intended. However when you navigate through a primary source like MDN for example, you're absorbing the domain of things that exist within your subject of study. Knowing what exists empowers you to ask better questions and iteratively refine your knowledge.

To help further explain, consider the skilled programmer from earlier. They know Java very well, but have never used Kotlin. They could try out Kotlin (JVM) and face no immediate friction, writing code that technically works. However, since they know the value of doing their homework, they skim the Kotlin docs for signs of unique syntax and stdlib symbols. They now know that Kotlin has distinct conventions regarding null and that they can use lateinit to better observe those conventions. It's important to build this instinct early, lest you feel compelled to vibe code a 50k LoC JS file because you haven't read the docs and antiquated tutorials neglect to address the advent of modules.

title_answer_45361327: What exactly does AI do beyond ML models and rule-based logic?
body_answer_45361327:
Not sure I can answer everything here, but let me see how I can help:

  1. The idea of AI systems is that it could be a interwoven pipeline of multiple models and steps.

    For example, imagine you want to classify texts in specific categories of your choosing. But to have supervised learning on it, you need all the data labeled with the categories you want. You don't want to go trough your millions of text snippets and label them. So, you can use unsupervised, like clustering, to separate your texts into piles of similar ones. Then you can label the clusters based on a limited number of samples that you actually read, and voila - you now have a labeled set for your supervised learning, with which you can continue. You just used two different ML models here, thus making it a system.

  2. That said, ML is a subset of AI - so all ML is AI, but not vice versa - even in your example you are talking about AI as ML+the rules. In that same manner LLMs, which we can consider AI, are the ML models used for NLP + the prompt engineering + the parameter tuning + ideally some decision making on reliability of the sources (like - don't use things you scrape from this list of websites, because they are not true) etc.

  3. On that point, decision making by AI can appear on any level - could be "don't use data based on this input", or "if the probability is higher than x, flag this", or "add this article to that cluster", or "ban this user", or "correct this text while it is being written" - they are all decisions, even if some have more real world impact than others. Decision making is a very broad term for "do something autonomously", where the something can be in any stage. Even a simple classification model that we use as a blackbox makes some decisions inside. (And that is why it is so hard to have those explainable - why did the ML model classify this input like that? And then it might be that you look into it, and it had 52% certainty, and you absolutely should not have based a whole project on it.).

Perhaps it could once more refer to the academic discipline, but once a term has reached popular culture, it largely means what non-specialists think it means.

title_answer_12506590: Is coding going to be obsolete?
body_answer_12506590:
Short answer: No.

Coding is a way to precisely describe to the compiler what it should do.
As you said, natural language is not precise enough to describe that, therefore we have the rigid, structured programming languages that essentially tell the compiler "Do this. Exactly this." - and the compiler, with zero creativity, following a similarly strict set of rules, does exactly as you told it (including any mistakes/bugs you included in your instructions).

Now let's switch the view to AI. AI, by both design and necessity, is not following a strict rule-set. Its outputs are not precisely predictable. Even if we pretend it could correctly "guess" at your intentions you still have the first problem: Precisely stating them.
Can you precisely "draw" your desired states and outcomes in a state diagram? "Click button to open window" still sounds easy, how about "Take this list of photos and sort them"... sort them how? Alphabetically? By Date? By image content? What exactly does take mean? You are giving your AI-Djinn a lot of wiggle-room here and, even if it is benign and tries to interpret your wish as correctly as possible - natural language is simply not precise enough.

To start with: strictly speaking, there is no any difference between randomly generated strings and strings generated by humans. Surprise! Here is why: for any given string, there is a non-zero probability of the case when this string was created using a random number generator. On the other hand, a person can always generate a string not containing any known names. Even if some known names are used, they can be artificially mangled.

Therefore, the problem as you put it is an ill-posed problem.

However, a statistical analysis can be performed on a big set of strings to attempt to find correlations. It is a well-know fact that people hardly can imitate randomly generated sequences, so statistical analysis can detect considerable difference. In particular, it happens because the intuitive feeling of randomness betrays people. For example, people consider repetitions and other regular patters highly unlikely, but in reality the probability of the generation of such regular patterns is probable enough.

body_answer_1241689:
One approach is to measure the likelihood of your text under some language model, possibly after some priming text ("prompt"). Since language models are trained on human text, they will naturally predict text sequences that are more likely to be produced by humans, and will therefore assign lower probabilities to text sequences that are somehow "not human". Any language model that is trained on enough text would work: it does not have to be an LLM, although you will probably get the most accurate results with an LLM.

As an example: given the priming text "The capital of Spain is ", the word "Madrid" would have very high likelihood, whereas the word "aisodjasjd92j23ewds" would have rather lower likelihood, and "8tBzVLlxVQGoCYs" would have even lower likelihood. (Note that because aisodjasjd92j23ewds was banged out on a keyboard, a large-enough language model is likely to be able to predict the later parts of the input with higher probability than pure chance).

You'll have to figure out a suitable prompt (you could, for example, try a very naive "The following word was written by a human: "), a suitable likelihood threshold, and normalization/correction for the length of the input and the frequency of its tokens.

body_answer_7869117:
There's no AI tool in the world currently which can guarantee to build you a fully working code sample (beyond the most simple of functions, anyway) without any mistakes. Since it's non-deterministic you can't even guarantee it'll write you the same code twice, given the same requirements! It also can't really innovate, but it entirely relies on piecing together things from content it has previously "learned" from and hoping that they make sense in the new context. It's still just a gigantic probability engine at the end of the day (albeit a pretty sophisticated one).

If you cannot understand most of the code the AI produces then you are running a big risk of there being underlying problems in the code that are not obvious from initial testing - e.g. security issues, performance problems, strange logic bugs. You also may have difficulty in maintaining and enhancing the code in future, especially if, as often happens, the AI cannot fully re-comprehend what it produced the first time round and is unable to update it correctly.

Ideally you will need to know how to test, debug, fix, deploy and maintain what it produces - or you will need to hire someone who has those skills to do it on your behalf. AI capabilities may well improve in the future in this area, but at the moment you can't expect to fully automate your coding process.

However, there is nothing wrong with vibe-coding as long as you are aware of these risks and limitations, and you therefore only deploy the vibe-coded software in scenarios where those should not pose a real-life problem.

title_answer_1498743: What are the best-practice architectural workflows for LLM-based contract compliance agents?
body_answer_1498743:
I would not make this primarily a multi-agent problem. I would model it as a bounded evidence workflow with LLM steps inside it.

First, build a document graph, not just a vector index. Each clause should have a stable ID, section path, text span, defined terms, parties, dates, jurisdiction, referenced clauses, and outbound/inbound cross-references. Retrieval should return clause IDs plus the small dependency neighborhood: referenced sections, definitions, exceptions, and amendments.

Second, separate extraction from judgment. Use the LLM to extract structured facts from each evidence packet: obligation, actor, condition, deadline, exception, governing policy, and cited clause IDs. Then run the compliance decision against that structured packet. For binary or repeatable policy checks, a decision table, rules engine, or ordinary deterministic code is usually better than asking an agent to “reason harder.”

Third, make every judgment emit a decision record:

  • policy ID and version
  • clause IDs used as evidence
  • extracted facts
  • cross-references followed
  • deterministic checks applied
  • LLM model/prompt version, if used
  • verdict: pass/fail/needs review/not enough evidence
  • unresolved references or ambiguity
  • reviewer handoff note

That record matters more than chain-of-thought. You need a reproducible explanation based on cited evidence and policy versions, not a hidden reasoning transcript.

For agentic loops, keep them bounded: max reference depth, max retrieval expansions, max retries, and explicit “needs human/legal review” exits. A second agent can be useful as a reviewer, but only if it receives a different task or evidence view. Two agents reading the same packet with similar prompts often produce correlated confidence, not true independence.

For latency, precompute the document graph and clause embeddings at ingestion time. At query time, retrieve candidate policy/clause packets, expand references deterministically, then run extraction/judgment only on the compact packet. Do not keep stuffing the whole contract into context.

Finally, for legal-tech work, the system should produce reviewable compliance candidates, not final legal determinations. The accountable reviewer should be able to inspect exactly which clauses and policy rules produced each result.

title_answer_1486097: How do I code without being completely dependent on AI?
body_answer_1486097:
Use less AI, rather than no AI.

First of, while we don't know how the AI bubble is going to unwind and while we don't know the long term societal effects of AI on white collar jobs, it's also unlikely that AI will go away entirely. Using no AI is likely going to put you at somewhat of a disadvantage. While using AI as a crutch is also going to leave you behind compared to people who can use it and still code. Using AI well, but having strong basics is going to be the sweet spot.

One approach is to use AI when appropriate but take deliberate steps to strengthen your own human brain.

Some options

  • pick a much smaller project and build it by hand.

  • next time you have a gnarly function to write? or new tool/approach to try out. open a new project, then write a proof of concept by hand. Something really simple, CLI-driven, with rudimentary unit test functionality. I used to do that already, when in a big codebase, to really isolate the new stuff and be able to understand it more deeply. An even more valuable approach given an LLM heavy context.

  • don't jump to the AI to correct compile errors / runtime exceptions / logic errors. Read through and understand what the compiler / runtime is telling you. Try to reason it out yourself first.

  • rather than using AI in your editor, agentic programming environment, use it online in a dialog with an LLM. As a mentor, not a intern programmer. Challenge it, ask it for links and do you own research and thinking. Use it to be a better architect.

    • what format is suitable for your DSL?

    • how is the app's help functionality best structured?

    • what are the pros and cons of using frameworks/approach X vs Y?

    • ask for pointers for a particular problem you have, including, again links and references. Then go and read the docs for yourself.

  • review, understand, critique and modify the LLM-generated code. Do you understand it? Do you see any instances where it's not best practices? Here's an example: I've been teaching myself Rust and the LLM wrote a massive match statement based on what value a given constant boolean flag has in all the sub-commands I had put in an Enum. But that match was based on the enum variant, not even the actual boolean flag. That was a code smell, to me. Instead, I thought about it and implemented a new function in the Command trait they implement. This function returns a struct that carries a struct of meta information, the boolean flag's value among others. In Python, I would have used introspection. But in Rust, having big match statements distributed throughout code seems less clean than each command "knowing" what it does and indicating that by populating a struct with its own capabilities. Is my way better? Even if it isn't I still had to reason through it myself and if it fails later then that will be wedged in my "coding history".

  • read documentation on your own, to supplement the handholding.

  • read more of other people's code. This is something I don't do enough of myself, but many of the really top programmers will tell you how much they've learned from others' code.

  • Desktop-based platforms could never create good web apps. The results were too heavyweight or took so much time to migrate, the apps were abandoned and rewritten.
  • Web platforms were terrible for mobile, even for mobile web.

Even well-written MDA applications couldn't handle the usage patterns of new platforms like web or mobile. Those usage patterns meant the data and processes changed as well.

Martin Fowler was skeptical about MDA and the CASE tools that predated it as far back as 2004

title_answer_18561482: Need advice on how to handle data and find groupings using ML/AI/DS
body_answer_18561482:
This is unsupervised text clustering, but TF-IDF + K-Means is the wrong tool for semantic grouping.

Why it fails

  • TF-IDF captures word frequency, not meaning

  • K-Means forces clusters and ignores context

  • You cluster common words, not how issues were fixed

What to do instead

  1. Use sentence embeddings (e.g. sentence-transformers, OpenAI embeddings)

  2. Cluster with HDBSCAN (no need to predefine k) or BERTopic

  3. Manually name the discovered clusters (unsupervised ≠ auto-labels)

Correct workflow

  • Discover clusters → review examples → assign labels like Software Upgrade, DB Fix

  • Optionally train a supervised model later

TL;DR: Change the text representation (embeddings), not the clustering algorithm.

  • Third: Changes will be fundamental for all knowledge workers. So you are right to worry. It is important to analyse the situation and adapt to it. But to be honest I would not worry too much, because ...

  • Employers will pay for the value you create for the company. How you do this - hand craft code or use AI is somewhat secondary.

  • With AI it is the same as with every other technology, we will first get rid of the boring and easy to automate tasks.

  • This shifts our (human) tasks to more conceptional work. Concretely this means, in my opinion, that for the future one really needs to have good skills regarding concepts. So, how to organize code properly, how to write clean code understand architecture. Know how requirements translate to the proper architecture. How to write efficient code, so to meet non functional requirements.
    Of course: The AI can help you with all of that, but it will not do everything automatically. You have to at least tell it and supervise the output. This will not go away.

  • Another not to underestimate skill we as future attractive employees need to have is really good communication and management skills. You need to manage your AI, give it tasks, steer it to the right direction, judge the output, set targets, plan projects in pieces. Know processes that work and lead to long-term(!) maintainable software. Ensure test coverage, ensure existence of meaningful tests. The big picture architecture of your codebase must be still in your head and all the key design choices. The little details not.
    This is way more difficult as it seems. I have experienced not everyone is able to write good, targeted prompts. And this is a communication skill, that you a) have clear thoughts and b) can express your thoughts clearly.

So TLDR:

  • You dont_ You accept dependency on AI. I wouldn't worry here too much. There is no company who has the monopoly. Similarly as we today depend on electricity, clean water supply, always filled supermarkets and so on...

  • Just make sure, you have the right skillsets to create value for your employer.
